q: What are the two variables whose relationship is given by the environmental Kuznets curve?
options: Environmental degradation and per capita income
solution:
The correct answer is Environmental degradation and per capita income.

Key Points

• Environmental Kuznets curve:

• The environmental Kuznets curve (EKC) is a relationship between environmental quality and economic development.

• According to this theory, many indicators of environmental degradation tend to get worse as modern economic growth occurs until average income reaches a certain point over the course of development.

• In other words, the environmental Kuznets curve suggests that economic development initially leads to a deterioration in the environment, but after a certain level of economic growth, a society begins to improve its relationship with the environment, and levels of environmental degradation reduce.

• The EKC suggests that the solution to pollution is economic growth.

Additional Information

• This is a debatable theory.

• The link between levels of income and environmental degradation is quite weak.

• It is possible economic growth will be compatible with an improved environment, but it requires a very deliberate set of policies and willingness to produce energy and goods in the most environmentally friendly way.

q: The process of wastewater treatment is commonly called  treatment.
solution:
The correct answer is sewage.

Key Points

• The process of wastewater treatment is commonly called sewage treatment.

• Cleaning of water is a process of removing pollutants before it enters a water body or is reused.

• There are mainly three types of sewage treatment stages primary, secondary or biological, and tertiary sewage treatments.

Additional Information

• Primary treatment (Physical process):

• It is the process of physically removing small and large particles from sewage.

• The floating debris is first removed by filtration through wire mesh screens in a sequential filtration.

• Secondary or biological sewage treatment:

• It is the removal of biodegradable organic matter from sewage or similar types of wastewater.

• This is usually done with the help of microorganisms, hence it is called biological treatment.

• Tertiary treatment (Chemical process):

• Biological treatment precedes chemical treatment in the treatment process.

• Chemical treatment is now considered as a tertiary treatment that can be more broadly defined as “treatment of wastewater by a process involving chemical treatment”.

q: refers to a sanitation system in which toilets collect human excreta in sealable, removable cartridges that are transported to treatment facilities.

Key Points

• Container-based sanitation (CBS) is a sanitation method in which toilets collect human waste and transport it to treatment facilities in sealable, removable containers (also known as cartridges).

• This method of sanitation entails the use of a commercial service that offers specific types of portable toilets and distributes empty containers when full ones are picked up. The service carries excreta and carefully disposes of or reuses it.

• The users are normally responsible for the cost of excreta collection. CBS can be utilised to offer low-income urban areas safe collection, transportation, and treatment of faeces at a lesser cost than establishing and maintaining sewers with the right development, support, and collaborations.

• Sanitation systems based on containers are a low-cost option. They can be employed in quickly increasing cities, refugee camps, and disaster relief circumstances.

• They are in line with Sustainable Development Goal 6 of the United Nations, which is to "provide sanitation for all by 2030."

Important Points

• Ecological sanitation is a method of sanitation that tries to safely reuse human waste in agriculture.

• It is a concept, not a technology or a device, that is defined by a goal to "complete the loop" between sanitation and agriculture in a safe manner, primarily for nutrients and organic matter.

• The disposal of human waste without the use of water as a carrier is known as dry sanitation.

• CLTS (Community Led Total Sanitation) is an innovative approach to mobilizing communities to prevent open defecation (OD). Communities are given the tools they need to assess and analyze open defecation (OD) and take steps to achieve ODF (open defecation free).

Additional Information

q:

(ii) Deterioration in the quality of soil

solution:

• Green Revolution:-

• It​ was a significant development in India's agricultural sector that aimed to increase agricultural productivity and reduce food insecurity.

• However, it also had some negative effects.

• Depletion of groundwater table:-

• The Green Revolution promoted the use of high-yielding crop varieties, which required more water for irrigation.

• As a result, farmers started extracting groundwater at an unsustainable rate, leading to a decline in the groundwater table.

• This, in turn, led to water scarcity and affected the livelihoods of farmers who depended on groundwater for irrigation.

• Deterioration in the quality of soil:-

• The use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides was a key feature of the Green Revolution.

• Over time, this led to soil degradation, loss of soil fertility, and reduced crop yields.

• Soil erosion, salinization, and acidification were some of the other negative impacts on soil quality.

• Increased input cost:-

• The adoption of new technologies and practices under the Green Revolution required farmers to invest in expensive inputs like seeds, fertilizers, and machinery.

• This increased the cost of cultivation, making it difficult for small and marginal farmers to afford these inputs.

• As a result, they had to borrow money from moneylenders at high-interest rates, leading to a cycle of debt and poverty.

Additional Information

• Green Revolution: It refers to the period of rapid agricultural development in the 1960s and 1970s, which aimed to increase food production through the use of high-yielding crop varieties, chemical fertilizers, and pesticides.

• Positive Effects: The Green Revolution led to a significant increase in food production, reduced food prices, and improved food security in India.

• It also created new job opportunities and increased rural income.

• Sustainable Agriculture: It refers to an agricultural system that is environmentally friendly, socially just, and economically viable.

• It promotes the use of organic farming practices, crop diversification, and conservation of natural resources.

q: Which of the following are the two basic categories of an ecosystem?

q: Which of the following is NOT a greenhouse gas?
solution:
The correct answer is Nitric oxide.

Key Points

• Nitric oxide (NO) is not considered a greenhouse gas because it does not have a significant impact on the Earth's temperature or climate.

• Greenhouse gases are those that can absorb and emit infrared radiation, leading to the greenhouse effect. Nitric oxide does not significantly contribute to this process.

• Common greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), and nitrous oxide (N2O), all of which have a much higher potential to trap heat in the atmosphere.

• Nitric oxide is primarily known for its role in the formation of smog and its impact on the respiratory system, rather than its role as a greenhouse gas.

Additional Information

• Greenhouse Gases:

• Greenhouse gases are those gases in the Earth's atmosphere that trap heat. They allow sunlight to enter the atmosphere freely, but when the Earth's surface emits the energy back as infrared radiation (heat), greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit this radiation, warming the planet.

• The primary greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere are water vapor (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), and ozone (O3).

• Human activities, such as burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial processes, have significantly increased the concentrations of these greenhouse gases, leading to global warming and climate change.

• Carbon Dioxide (CO2):

• Carbon dioxide is a colorless, odorless gas that is essential for plant life through the process of photosynthesis.

• It is produced by the combustion of fossil fuels, deforestation, and various industrial processes.

• CO2 is the most significant long-lived greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere, contributing to global warming and climate change.

• Methane (CH4):

• Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential many times greater than that of CO2 over a 20-year period.

• It is produced naturally through the decomposition of organic matter and human activities such as livestock farming, rice cultivation, and landfills.

• Despite its shorter atmospheric lifetime compared to CO2, methane's impact on global warming is substantial.

• Nitrous Oxide (N2O):

• Nitrous oxide is a greenhouse gas that is more effective than CO2 at trapping heat in the atmosphere over a 100-year period.

• It is emitted from agricultural and industrial activities, as well as during the combustion of fossil fuels and solid waste.

• N2O also plays a role in the depletion of the ozone layer in the stratosphere.

q: Which of the following is the best definition of ecological efficiency?
options: The amount of energy utilised at different trophic levels in a food chain
The amount of energy stored at different trophic levels in a food chain
The ratio between the mass and the energy flow at different trophic levels in a food chain
The ratio between energy flows at different points in a food chain
solution:
The correct answer is The ratio between energy flows at different points in a food chain.

Key Points

• Ecological efficiency refers to the efficiency with which energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next in a food chain.

• Typically, only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next level; this is known as the 10% law.

• This concept helps in understanding the energy dynamics and the structure of ecosystems.

• Higher trophic levels receive less energy, which explains why there are typically fewer organisms at higher levels in a food chain.

Additional Information

• Trophic Levels

• In ecology, a trophic level is the position that an organism occupies in a food chain.

• Primary producers (plants) are at the first trophic level, primary consumers (herbivores) at the second, secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) at the third, and so on.

• Energy Flow

• Energy flow in an ecosystem is one-way: from the sun to producers, then to consumers, and finally to decomposers.

• Energy is lost at each trophic level, primarily as heat resulting from metabolism.

• 10% Law

• The 10% law states that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level.

• This rule was first introduced by Raymond Lindeman in 1942.

• Food Chain

• A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms through which nutrients and energy pass as one organism eats another.

• In a food chain, each organism occupies a different trophic level.

q: Which international treaty was adopted in 1992 to combat global warming and prepare for its effects?

United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
solution:
The correct answer is United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

Key Points

• It serves as the foundation for global efforts to combat climate change and has been ratified by 197 parties, including nearly all countries worldwide.

• The UNFCCC led to the establishment of the annual Conference of the Parties (COP), where nations meet to negotiate and review progress in addressing climate change.

Additional Information

• Kyoto Protocol:

• A landmark international treaty adopted under the UNFCCC in 1997 and came into force in 2005.

• It legally binds developed countries to emission reduction targets.

• It introduced market-based mechanisms like emissions trading, clean development mechanism (CDM), and joint implementation (JI).

• Paris Agreement:

• An agreement within the UNFCCC adopted in 2015 and came into force in 2016.

• It aims to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, preferably to 1.5 degrees Celsius, compared to pre-industrial levels.

• Countries submit nationally determined contributions (NDCs) outlining their climate actions.

• Green Climate Fund (GCF):

• Established under the UNFCCC in 2010 to assist developing countries in adaptation and mitigation practices to counter climate change.

• Aims to mobilize $100 billion per year by 2020 from various sources.

• Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC):

• Provides scientific assessments on climate change to inform policy decisions.

• Established in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).

q: A coastal city implements a plan to build sea walls and elevate buildings in response to rising sea levels. This action primarily falls under which category of climate change response?
solution:
The correct answer is Climate Change Adaptation.

Key Points

• Climate Change Adaptation refers to measures taken to adjust to the current or expected effects of climate change in order to minimize harm or exploit beneficial opportunities.

• The construction of sea walls and elevation of buildings specifically addresses the impacts of rising sea levels, which are a direct consequence of climate change. These are preventive actions to safeguard infrastructure and human lives.

• Adaptation strategies are often localized and cater to the specific challenges posed by climate change, such as floods, droughts, or temperature increases.

• The goal of adaptation is to build resilience in communities, economies, and ecosystems, allowing them to cope with the adverse effects of climate change.

• This approach differs from mitigation, which focuses on reducing the causes of climate change, such as greenhouse gas emissions.

Additional Information

• Climate Change Mitigation:

• Mitigation involves efforts to reduce or prevent the emission of greenhouse gases (GHGs) that contribute to global warming.

• Examples include switching to renewable energy sources like solar or wind, increasing energy efficiency, and adopting sustainable transportation practices.

• This strategy aims to address the root cause of climate change rather than its effects.

• For instance, the Paris Agreement focuses on mitigation by setting targets for reducing global GHG emissions.

• Carbon Sequestration:

• It refers to the process of capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) to reduce its concentration in the atmosphere.

• Natural methods include afforestation, reforestation, and soil management, while technological solutions include carbon capture and storage (CCS).

• Carbon sequestration is a key component of climate change mitigation strategies, aimed at offsetting emissions from industrial processes.

• Geoengineering:

• Geoengineering involves large-scale interventions in Earth's natural systems to counteract climate change.

• Examples include solar radiation management (reflecting sunlight back into space) and ocean fertilization to enhance carbon capture by marine ecosystems.

• These methods are controversial due to their potential unintended consequences and ethical concerns.

• Examples of Climate Change Adaptation:

• Constructing flood barriers in coastal cities prone to rising sea levels.

• Implementing drought-resistant crops in regions experiencing water scarcity due to climate changes.

• Developing early warning systems for extreme weather events such as hurricanes or heatwaves.

• Retrofitting infrastructure to withstand extreme weather conditions, such as stronger buildings to resist cyclones.

Important Points

• Rising Sea Levels:

• Sea levels have been rising globally due to melting ice caps and glaciers, as well as the thermal expansion of seawater caused by global warming.

• According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), global sea levels could rise by 0.3 to 1 meter by 2100.

• This poses threats to low-lying and coastal areas, leading to increased flooding, erosion, and loss of habitats.

• Global Adaptation Efforts:

• The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) emphasizes the need for adaptation measures alongside mitigation strategies.

• Programs like the Global Environment Facility (GEF) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) provide financial support for adaptation projects in developing countries.

• Several nations, including the Netherlands, have implemented large-scale adaptation projects such as flood management systems and sustainable urban planning.

q: What astronomical observation is most severely hampered by increasing levels of urban light pollution?
solution:
The correct answer is Deep-sky objects.

Key Points

• Deep-sky objects refer to astronomical entities such as galaxies, nebulae, star clusters, and distant celestial objects that are faint and require dark skies for observation.

• Urban light pollution significantly hampers the visibility of deep-sky objects by increasing the sky brightness, reducing contrast, and obscuring faint objects.

• Light pollution from artificial sources, such as streetlights and buildings, scatters in the atmosphere, overwhelming the faint light emitted by deep-sky objects.

• Observing deep-sky objects typically requires remote locations or observatories situated far from urban areas to minimize the effects of light pollution.

• Efforts to mitigate light pollution, including the use of shielded lighting and adherence to dark-sky standards, are crucial for preserving the visibility of deep-sky objects.

Additional Information

• Sunspots

• Sunspots are dark, cooler areas on the Sun's surface caused by magnetic activity that inhibits convection.

• Observing sunspots does not typically require dark skies, as they can be seen using solar filters or telescopes during the daytime.

• Urban light pollution does not significantly affect the observation of sunspots, as they are observed against the bright background of the Sun.

• Planetary Transit

• Planetary transit occurs when a planet passes in front of its host star, causing a temporary dip in the star's brightness.

• These events are usually studied using telescopes equipped with photometers or spectrometers, and they are not as affected by light pollution as deep-sky objects.

• However, precise measurements of brightness changes may require optimal conditions, which can be influenced by urban light pollution.

• Lunar Phases

• Lunar phases refer to the appearance of the Moon as it orbits Earth, changing its illuminated portion visible from Earth.

• Light pollution has minimal impact on observing lunar phases because the Moon is bright enough to be visible even in urban environments.

• Lunar observation is often used as an introductory activity for amateur astronomers due to its ease of visibility.

• Light Pollution and Astronomy

• Light pollution refers to the excessive and misdirected artificial light that disrupts natural darkness, impacting astronomical observations.

• It reduces the visibility of faint celestial objects and interferes with professional and amateur astronomy.

• Organizations like the International Dark-Sky Association (IDA) advocate for measures to reduce light pollution through responsible lighting practices.

q:

Key Points

• PM2.5 particles are more harmful than PM10 because they are smaller and can penetrate deeper into the respiratory system, reaching the lungs and even entering the bloodstream.

• PM2.5 refers to particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or smaller, whereas PM10 refers to particles with a diameter of 10 micrometers or smaller.

• Due to their smaller size, PM2.5 particles remain suspended in the air for longer durations and are more likely to be inhaled by humans.

• Exposure to PM2.5 is associated with severe health risks, including respiratory diseases, cardiovascular issues, and even premature death, as these particles can directly impact vital organs by traveling through the bloodstream.

• The Air Quality Index (AQI) considers PM2.5 as a critical pollutant due to its severe health implications, making it a significant parameter in assessing air quality.

Additional Information

q: The UN Sustainable Development Report 2024 primarily tracks progress towards which global goals?
solution:
The correct answer is Sustainable Development Goals.

Key Points

• Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted by the United Nations Member States in 2015 as a universal call to action to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure peace and prosperity for all by 2030.

• The SDGs consist of 17 goals and 169 targets, aimed at addressing a wide range of global challenges, including poverty, inequality, climate change, environmental degradation, and justice.

• The UN Sustainable Development Report 2024 primarily tracks progress made towards achieving these goals by analyzing data from countries and presenting an annual assessment of efforts and outcomes.

• Each goal under the SDGs is interconnected, emphasizing the need for coordinated actions across sectors such as health, education, energy, and environmental sustainability.

• The report utilizes tools like the Sustainable Development Goals Index to rank countries based on their performance towards achieving the SDGs, encouraging international collaboration and accountability.

Additional Information

• Millennium Development Goals (MDGs):

• The MDGs were a precursor to the SDGs and focused on eight goals to combat poverty, hunger, disease, illiteracy, environmental degradation, and discrimination by 2015.

• While significant progress was made under the MDGs, they were criticized for their limited scope, which led to the broader and more inclusive framework of the SDGs.

• Environmental Protection Goals:

• These goals are often part of larger frameworks like the SDGs, focusing on issues such as climate action, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable resource management.

• While they are critical, they are not the primary focus of the UN Sustainable Development Report 2024, which tracks the SDGs comprehensively.

• Human Rights Goals:

• The SDGs incorporate elements of human rights, such as gender equality, reduced inequality, and justice, making them a universal framework that aligns closely with human rights principles.

• However, human rights goals as a standalone category are not directly tracked by the UN Sustainable Development Report.

• Sustainable Development Goals Index:

• The SDG Index ranks countries annually based on their progress toward achieving the 17 SDGs.

• It uses metrics such as healthcare access, education quality, renewable energy use, and environmental conservation to evaluate performance.

• This index is a central feature of the UN Sustainable Development Report.

Important Points

• Key Features of the SDGs:

• The SDGs apply to all countries, emphasizing universal goals rather than being limited to developing nations.

• They integrate social, economic, and environmental dimensions of sustainable development.

• Each goal has specific indicators and targets to measure progress.

• Global Partnerships:

• The SDGs highlight the importance of collaborative efforts across governments, NGOs, private sector, and academia.

• Goal 17 specifically emphasizes Partnerships for the Goals to mobilize resources for achieving the targets.

• Challenges in Implementation:

• Challenges include data availability, financing gaps, political will, and global inequalities.

• The UN Sustainable Development Report provides insights and recommendations to address these challenges.

Regarding the legal protection of Dugong (Sea Cow) in India, consider the following statements:
Statement 1: The Dugong is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Statement 2: This classification provides the Dugong with the highest level of legal protection, similar to that of the Tiger.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is Both Statement 1 and Statement 2.

Key Points

• Statement 1: The Dugong (Sea Cow) is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, which ensures the highest level of legal protection for species in India. *Hence, Statement 1 is correct.*

• Statement 2: Being included under Schedule I means Dugong receives the same level of protection as the Tiger, as both are considered critically important for conservation. *Hence, Statement 2 is correct.*

• The Dugong is a marine herbivorous mammal, classified as vulnerable globally under the IUCN Red List. In India, its conservation is a priority due to its declining population.

• Legal protection under Schedule I prohibits activities like hunting, capturing, or harming Dugongs, and violators face stringent penalties under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

• The Dugong’s habitat, predominantly in shallow coastal waters like the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands, further necessitates robust legal protection.

Additional Information

• Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972:

• It is a comprehensive law enacted to protect wildlife and their habitats in India.

• Species under Schedule I enjoy the maximum protection, with penalties for violations including fines and imprisonment.

• The Act also provides provisions for the establishment of protected areas like National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.

• Dugong Conservation:

• The Dugong’s population in India is threatened by habitat loss, hunting, and accidental entanglement in fishing nets.

• Several conservation initiatives like the Dugong Recovery Program have been launched to protect its population and habitat.

• Dugongs are primarily found in the Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park, which is a critical conservation site.

• Comparison with Tiger Conservation:

• Both Dugong and Tiger are listed under Schedule I, ensuring the highest level of protection.

• Tiger conservation has seen success through programs like Project Tiger, which serves as a model for Dugong conservation strategies.

• The focus on habitat restoration and community involvement is crucial for both species.

• Threats to Dugongs:

• Destruction of seagrass beds, which are the primary food source for Dugongs.

• Pollution and sedimentation affecting coastal ecosystems.

• Illegal hunting and fishing practices.

Important Points

• Global Status: Dugongs are classified as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and are protected under Appendix I of CITES.

• Habitat: Dugongs inhabit shallow waters of tropical and subtropical regions, relying heavily on seagrass meadows.

• Government Initiatives: India has implemented measures like habitat restoration, awareness campaigns, and collaboration with local communities to protect Dugongs.

• International Conservation: The Dugong is a focus of international conservation efforts, including the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS).
